# For visual artists

A picture here is a field of lights. Each light is a coin that keeps being tossed, with a bias toward the picture
it wants to be and a pull toward its neighbours. Out of noise the picture forms, holds, breaks up again when the
field is heated, and forms again. SETTLE is the language that describes such a field. KANERVA is a memory that
stores pictures as bit patterns and brings one back from a smudged copy. settle-mcp hands both to an assistant,
so you can ask for a program instead of writing one.

## What this is

The visual work done with these tools so far:

- [The film player](#/film) takes a film frame by frame and lets the field settle toward each frame. It shows every
  stage: the target, the leans, the live coins, the bits read, the soft read, the error map. Under TRUE TIME RENDER
  the film keeps its own pace and the field in front catches up as fast as the machine allows, skipping frames when
  it must, so the picture on screen is always close to the frame the clock is at.
- The footer of every page is two layers of the brain drawn as lights, the cortex in six layers above the
  cerebellum below, with spikes running along the wires. A click rides into the Purkinje forest with a game's
  camera.
- [The SDMMEMORY page](#/sdmmemory) stores letters as valleys in a Hopfield net, adds noise to one, and watches it come
  back; the same page shows a room of Kanerva hard locations and a dial from a hard memory to attention.

The drawing library is [settle-see](#/settlesee). It has no dependencies, draws on a canvas,
colours every light by the SETTLE neon code (ten neons, each meaning one thing in the physics), and settles into a
word, a registered shape, an SVG path, your own canvas drawing, a picture read by brightness, or a raw bit array.
Its README lists the shapes: a physics family (`purkinje`, `landscape`, `tanh`, `spins`, `boltzmann`, `hopfield`,
`sdm`, `hypercube`, and the painted `cortex6`, `cerebellum`, `brainbands`), a plain family (`circle`, `ring`,
`heart`, `star`, `spiral`, `wave`, `cross`, `diamond`, `moon`, `eye`), and a credits family.

## How you can use it in your project

### SETTLE alone

SETTLE's `grid` family makes a picture out of things, one per pixel, each leaning toward the grey of the source and
pulled toward its four neighbours. One settle gives one noisy sample; forty settles averaged give a cleaned
picture. The program writes a PGM you can open in any image editor. That is a denoiser, a texture generator and a
film grain, depending on the temperature and the pull you choose.

### KANERVA alone

A 256-bit pattern is a 16 by 16 tile. KANERVA stores thousands of such tiles in one memory, spread across every
hard location, and brings one back from a copy with a fifth of its bits flipped. A memory like that is an
instrument for an installation: show it a scrawl, get back the stored image it is nearest to, or get back `nothing
clear` when the scrawl is too far from anything it knows. The memory can also refuse: it says "I never stored that"
when a read-address travels too far ([KANERVA](#/kanerva)).

### SETTLE and KANERVA together

The memory is a settle. In SETTLE a stored pattern lives in the pulls between things, and a recall is the field
settling from a noisy start into the nearest valley. So a picture can be stored, recalled, heated until it breaks
and cooled until it returns, all in one program and one field of lights. The site's hero does this with words:
`<Settle morph>` hands the running field new targets and the lights settle toward them instead of restarting.

## An example

The picture program from the tutorial, run on 2026-10-02 with the release binary on the horse frame (150 by 100
pixels, 15,000 things).

```settle file=picture.settle
model :picture do
  grid :img, width: 150, height: 100, smooth: 0.2
  img.lean_from "horse.pgm", by: 1, correct: :yes
end

run :picture do
  settle 1, seed: 1
  img.show_as "one_sample.pgm", from: :last
  settle 40, seed: 1
  img.show_as "forty_samples.pgm", from: :rate
end
```

```text output=03_picture
settled: 1 samples of 15000 things at temperature 1
show_as :img -> one_sample.pgm (last), PSNR 7.95 dB against the leans' picture
settled: 40 samples of 15000 things at temperature 1
show_as :img -> forty_samples.pgm (rate), PSNR 24.46 dB against the leans' picture
```

One sample is a snow of coins at 7.95 dB; the rate over forty samples is the horse at 24.46 dB. The whole run took
0.02 s. The film player's curve has the same shape: on the Muybridge horse at 150 by 100, the soft read
at smooth 0.2 reaches 22.73 dB at 5 sweeps per frame and 28.79 dB at 80, and the player ran at 454.7 frames per
second at 10 sweeps on a loaded laptop, one thread ([the GRIDPLAYER result](#/results/gridplayer)).

## Getting started

1. Look first. Open [the film player](#/film) and move the sweeps slider; open [SDMMEMORY](#/sdmmemory) and damage a
   letter; open [WHAT?](#/what) and read the picture step, where the horse frame settles under TRUE TIME RENDER in the middle of the page.
2. Draw your own field. settle-see is plain JavaScript with no build step. Clone it
   beside your page (`git clone https://github.com/triplesparkle/settle-see`) and write:

```js
import { settle } from './settle-see/src/index.js';

const handle = settle(canvas, { image: 'my-picture.png', res: 192, neon: 'mem', color: 'single' });
handle.show(bits);   // settle into a new target now
```

   `res` is how many lights across; `color: 'meaning'` paints by the physics, `color: 'single'` uses one neon. A
   `{ draw: (c, w, h) => {} }` item settles into your own canvas drawing. The React form is
   `<Settle shape="purkinje" res={200} height={320} />` from `settle-see/react`.
3. Make a film. The site's film tool, `tools/make_hero_film.mjs` in the settle-site repository, turns a video or a folder of frames into the two-file
   film format settle-see plays (`<name>.json` and `<name>.bin`); a film item in a settle plays it on TRUE TIME,
   one frame every `1000 / fps` ms.
4. Print a picture from a program. Build the interpreter (`git clone https://github.com/triplesparkle/SETTLE`,
   `cd SETTLE`, `cargo build --release`), put a PGM beside the picture program above, run it, and open the PGMs it writes.
5. Ask the assistant. With settle-mcp added to Claude Code, ask for a program that stores three 16 by 16 tiles in
   a memory and recalls one from a damaged copy; the `sdm_store_recall` tool writes and runs it and shows the program.
